parties:
Ramchandra Saha & another
Vs.
Malay Baran Kundu & others
full_judgment:
2. Facts giving rise to the Rule, in short, is that opposite party no. 1 as petitioner filed Miscellaneous Case No. 128 of 1969 under Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act for preemption of the case land contending, inter alia, that he is the co-sharer of the disputed Joma which was sold and transferred by one Mahadeb Kundu, another co-sharer to Khokan Chandra predecessor of the present petitioners by a registered Kabala dated 13.6.1969 who was a stranger-purchaser. He further contends that a notice u/s 89 of the Act was served upon him as required under the law and thereafter he filed the case for preemption after obtaining the certified copy of the Kabala. 

 7. The learned Munsif found that the pre-emptor-petitioner opposite party no. 1 is admittedly co-sharer of the disputed Joma and he filed the Miscellaneous Case under Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act on receipt of notice under section 89 of the Act served upon him by the preemptor petitioner (purchaser) within time. The learned Munsif, however, dismissed the Miscellaneous case holding from the facts, evidence and circumstances of the case and relying on a decision in a case between Forman Ali Howlader Vs. Helaluddin and others, reported in 20 D.L.R. (1968) 1197 that the case is not maintainable under Section 96 of the Sate Acquisition and Tenancy Act as the disputed land is a non-agricultural land. On the other hand the learned Subordinate Judge allowed the Miscellaneous case allowing the appeal preferred by the preemptor-petitioner on reversing and setting aside the judgment and order passed by the learned Munsif holding that the transfer by the impugned Kabala was held as agricultural land and that the case be decided on the contents and recitals of the Kabala. The learned Subordinate Judge also relied on the ruling given in the case between Jadav Chandra Mali Vs. Abdul Khaleque and others, reported in 27 D.L.R.(AD) 114 holding that the ruling reported in 20 D.L.R. page 1197 relied by the learned Munsif is not applicable present case. 

 8. Admittedly the pre-emptor-petitioner is a co-sharer in respect of the disputed Joma and he was served with a notice u/s 89 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as required under the law and he filed the miscellaneous case under Section 96 of the said Act producing the case Kabala marked Ext. 1. In the Kabala the case land has also been admittedly described as agricultural land. But the contesting pre-emptee-opposite parties denied the same stating in their written objection that the deed writer wrongly mentioned the case land as agricultural land in the Kabala. 

 9. The definite case of the pre-emptee-opposite parties is that the disputed plot is a part of hat and Bazar, which is a 'Chandina', and the same is not agricultural land. On such facts and evidence the learned Munsif dismissed the Miscellaneous case as not maintainable under Section 96 of the SAT Act. The facts of the case he relied as reported in 20 D.L.R. is that a contiguous land owner sought pre-emption of the case land under Section 96 of the E.B. SAT Act which was a non-agricultural land. It was held in the case that "preemption in respect of non-agricultural land can be claimed only under the provisions of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and not under sec. 96 of the State Acquisition Act." The learned Munsif dismissed the case on the facts and evidence of the case and relying on the above decision. But the learned Subordinate Judge allowed the miscellaneous case on appeal holding that "in the present case the transfer has been held as agricultural land and since pre-emption is held on the kabala the 0.P. respondents are bound by the contents of that kabala". He also held relying on the decision reported in 27 DLR (AD) 114 that "mere section does not preclude the petitioner from preempting the case land". 

 10. The facts of the case reported in 27 DLR (AD) is, in short, that the pre-emptor petitioner filed an application under Section 96 of the E.B. S.A.T. Act for pre-emption of certain lands which was contested by the pre-emptee-opposite parties contending, inter alia, that the said land being 'chandina land' within a Municipal area the application under Section 96 of the Act had no application to the purchase in question. The case was allowed by the trial Court, which was affirmed by the Subordinate Judge on appeal, preferred by the pre-emptee-opposite party. He then filed an application under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the High Court Division and during pendency of the application a petition was filed on behalf of the pre-emptor under Order 6, rule 17 read with Section 151 and Section 153 of the C.P.C. for amendment of the application for preemption whereby the application for pre-emption u/s 96 of the SAT Act was sought to be converted to an application under Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act which was rejected by the High Court on the ground that it would change the nature of the case. In an appeal against the said judgment and order by the pre-emptor the Appellate Division held that "In the circumstances we find that the learned Judges were not justified in rejecting the prayer for amendment of the application upon the view they took. Moreover, since the relief prayed for could be given by the Court under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, even if that section had not been specifically mentioned in the application, it was not necessary either to apply for amendment for a change of description in the cause title." The Appellate Division also referred a decision reported in (1967) 19 DLR 347- P.L.D. 1967 (Dacca) 588, in its judgment where it was held that: - 

 "If the relief claimed by the petitioner was allowable under some other law of the country, namely, section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, then the Court of appeal below was bound to apply the same notwithstanding the misdescription of the cause title in the application." 

 11. Here in the case before me the disputed land was described in the recital of the Kabala as agricultural land and a notice was served upon the pre-emptor-petitioner under Section 89 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act leading him to file the Miscellaneous case under section 96 of the Act on depositing the required money for pre-emption of the case land. Although the contesting opposite parties did not claim that the case land is within any Municipal area nor there is any evidence on record that the alleged "Arot Ghar" were constructed before transfer of the case land, the learned Munsif dismissed the Miscellaneous case holding that the same is a "Chandina" and non-agricultural land and as such the pre-emptor-petitioner is not entitled to get any relief as prayed for u/s 96 of the Act. This view of the trial Court is wrong in view of the fact that the case land had been described in the recital of the impugned kabala as agricultural land and a notice u/s 89 of the SAT Act was served upon the pre-emptor. No step was taken to correct the impugned kabala. Nature and character of the case land as described in the recital and schedule of the impugned kabala governs the provisions of law attracting the right of pre-emption. Moreover, following the decision in the case between Abdul Hamid Kazi Versus Abdul Jabbar Jamadar & others reported in 26 DLR (SC) 681 also hold that, it is not the technicality of the cause title but the substance of the issue in controversy to be looked into, to resolve a dispute in issue between the parties to ensure proper justice. In conformity with decision reported in 27 DLR (AD) 114, I am also of the opinion that even if the case land in questions was a 'chandina' land, the trial court could very well grant the relief u/s 24 of the Non Agricultural Tenancy Act the pre-emptor originally sought in the case u/s 96 of the SAT Act. The learned Munsif was competent to allow the Miscellaneous case in the facts, evidence and circumstances of the case u/s 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act even without any amendment substituting Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act for section 96 of SAT Act. The appellate court below has rightly allowed the Miscellaneous case on reversing and setting aside the judgment and order of the learned Munsif relying on the above decision reported in 27 DLR. In that view of the matter I find no reason or ground to interfere with the judgment and order of the appellate Court below, as the learned Subordinate Judge did not commit any error of law resulting in an error in the decision causing failure of justice in allowing the appeal.
